extracted.intended_audience: design applicants, in-house counsel, IP agents and small businesses seeking international industrial design protection
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for filing and managing international industrial design registrations under the WIPO Hague System, plus related practical criteria for choosing filing routes, preparing applications, and maintaining design rights across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant eligibility for Hague System
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible, the applicant must be: a national or resident of a contracting party; a national of a member state of a contracting party; or have a real and effective business presence in a contracting party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure at least one of these links to a contracting party exists before filing internationally under the Hague System.

rubrics_metrics.name: Languages of filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The application may be filed in English, French, or Spanish, the official languages of the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare application materials in one of these three languages to avoid translation requirements at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of fees to pay
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must pay three types of fees (in Swiss francs): 1) a basic fee, 2) designation fees for each selected country, and 3) a publication fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for all three fee categories when comparing Hague vs national filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-designs per application limit and class requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A single application can include up to 100 designs, provided they all belong to the same class of the Locarno Classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group only designs in the same Locarno class; otherwise you may need to split applications or risk objections in some jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphic representation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each design must be accompanied by at least one reproduction—this could be a photo, drawing, or another type of graphic representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, high-quality views; consistency across views helps avoid formal or substantive problems during national examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some countries restrict multiple-design filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Some countries don't allow multiple designs in a single application. In such cases, the application may need to be divided when examined in that jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Division at national stage does not affect the international registration, but anticipate possible extra costs and procedures in those jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority claim time limit for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: You can claim priority from an earlier application (under the Paris Convention or WTO) if your international filing is submitted within six months of the earlier one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File within six months of your earlier design filing to preserve priority; missing this window forfeits the priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: WIPO formal examination scope
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO examines the application for compliance with formal requirements, such as the payment of fees and the quality of the design representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO does not perform substantive examination — expect only formal compliance checks at the international level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing and options
rubrics_metrics.description: The application is published in the International Designs Bulletin—usually six months after filing. Applicants can request early publication or deferment of publication (where allowed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider early publication or deferment based on commercial strategy and national law interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated national substantive examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Designated national IP offices are then notified and will conduct substantive examinations in accordance with their national laws. WIPO does not perform substantive examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction substantive review and potential refusals or objections after international publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of national decisions / effect of refusals
rubrics_metrics.description: Each designated contracting party decides independently whether to grant protection. If a design is refused in one jurisdiction, it does not affect the application's status in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each refusal as a national matter; a favorable outcome in some jurisdictions does not guarantee outcomes elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal issue time limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusals must be issued within either 6 or 12 months from the date of publication, depending on the applicable national laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check each designated country’s refusal period to know when protection will be deemed granted if no refusal is issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection deemed granted if no refusal within time limit
rubrics_metrics.description: If no refusal is issued within the prescribed time limit, protection is deemed to be granted in that jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor national office communications and published timelines so you know when rights have taken effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses to national refusals handled locally
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to refusals are handled directly between the applicant and the national IP office—not through WIPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to instruct local counsel or agents to prosecute refusals and handle substantive arguments in each jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial validity and renewals under Hague international registration
rubrics_metrics.description: International design protection is initially valid for five years from the filing date. It can be renewed for additional five-year terms, up to the maximum duration permitted under the laws of each designated contracting party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renewals at the international level are in five-year increments but overall duration depends on designated countries’ maxima; plan renewals accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: WIPO renewal reminders
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO will remind the right holder six months before renewal is due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use WIPO reminders but maintain your own docketing system—don't rely solely on reminders from WIPO.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to choose Hague vs national filings
rubrics_metrics.description: It's usually best when you want design protection in multiple Hague members and prefer a centralized filing and renewal workflow. If you only need 1-2 countries (or key markets are not covered by the Hague System), national filings may be simpler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess number of target countries, whether key markets are Hague members, and administrative preferences before choosing the route.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to choose which countries to designate
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with where you will manufacture, sell, ship, or face copying risk in the next 2-3 years. Hague application lets you designate as few or as many members as you want, so most applicants focus on core markets first and expand strategically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align designation choices with commercial plans and enforcement priorities rather than filing everywhere by default.

rubrics_metrics.name: No national filing pre-requirement for Hague
rubrics_metrics.description: No, according to WIPO, there is no pre-requirement to file nationally or regionally before filing the Hague application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hague can be used as a 'global-first' route; still consider priority strategies where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application preparation to avoid delays/refusals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clean, consistent views in the application, and avoid contradictions between views. Ensure the product indication and Locarno classification align.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality and consistency of images and indications are key formal and substantive elements—poor or contradictory representations can trigger objections or refusals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budgeting Hague vs national filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare one Hague filing with selected designations versus national filings in the same countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider basic + designation + publication fees vs multiple national application fees and translation/agent costs when budgeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: General renewal management principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Because renewal procedures vary widely across jurisdictions, it’s essential to monitor deadlines and fee requirements closely. Failure to renew on time can result in the loss of valuable design rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement jurisdiction-specific renewal calendars and monitor grace periods and surcharges to avoid lapses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country-specific renewal rules — South Korea
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity: 20 years from the filing date. Initial Payment: Registration fee due within 3 months of receiving the Notice of Allowance; covers the first 3 years. Ongoing Payments: Annual renewal fees are required from year 4 onward, paid before the anniversary of the registration date with grace period of 6 months for late payment with a surcharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note Korea’s mix of an initial multi-year payment followed by annual renewals from year 4; calendar and grace terms differ from other jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country-specific renewal rules — China
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity: 15 years for designs filed on or after June 1, 2021; 10 years for designs filed before that date. Initial Payment: Grant fee due within 2 months of receiving the Notice of Grant. Ongoing Payments: Annual fees due before the filing date anniversary. A 6-month grace period is available for late payments (with surcharge). A stamp tax is also required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of China’s change in term in 2021 and additional formalities (stamp tax).

rubrics_metrics.name: Country-specific renewal rules — United States
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity: 15 years for design patents filed on or after May 13, 2015; 14 years for design patents filed before that date. Unlike most countries, U.S. design patents do not require renewal fees or annuities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: US design patent term and no renewal requirement is distinct; consider national patent vs design route implications for the U.S. market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country-specific renewal rules — European Union (EUIPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage: Single application provides protection across all EU Member states. Initial validity: 5 years from the date of filing. Renewals: Up to four additional 5-year periods (maximum of 25 years). Late renewal is allowed within a 6-month grace period (with a surcharge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EU design protection centralizes coverage; renewal structure differs from some national systems—plan maximum term strategy accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country-specific renewal rules — ARIPO
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage: select African countries. Initial validity: 10 years from the date of filing. Renewals: Renewal fees due annually on the filing date anniversary and should be paid separately for each designated country. Late renewal is allowed within a 6-month grace period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ARIPO’s model requires annual renewals per designated country—administrative implications for portfolio management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design protection substantive criteria (varies by jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Varying slightly in different countries, the basic requirements for design protection are novelty and individual character (EU and Australia), sometimes complemented by the requirement of creativity (Japan), ornamentality (USA) or other such criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the substantive standard in each target jurisdiction (novelty, individual character, creativity, ornamentality) before filing and when drafting representations to meet those local thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a design is worth registering
rubrics_metrics.description: A design can be worth registering if a consumer can easily distinguish the design of your product from other products in the same category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate commercial distinctiveness and enforcement value—if consumers can easily distinguish your product’s appearance, registration may be justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model eligibility criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility model usually only needs to meet two criteria: novelty (the invention must be new) and industrial applicability (it must be capable of being made or used in industry). Inventive step is often not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility models are jurisdiction-specific; verify whether the target jurisdiction allows utility models and any technology restrictions (e.g., mechanical devices only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model procedural and strategic advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike patents, substantive examination is often not required, making utility models faster to obtain. They are generally more affordable and simpler to obtain than standard patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use utility models when fast, lower-cost protection for incremental innovations with short commercial lifespan is preferable to longer-term patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to choose utility model vs patent
rubrics_metrics.description: They are best suited when: the invention has a short commercial lifespan; the improvement is incremental rather than revolutionary; fast protection is more important than long-term coverage; budget constraints make patent protection less practical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess commercial lifecycle, novelty vs inventive_step needs, and jurisdictional availability when choosing between utility model and patent routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to decide countries for utility model filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with where you'll manufacture, sell, ship, or expect copying, then check whether each target jurisdiction even offers utility models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only file utility models in countries that offer them and align with your commercial footprint and enforcement needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common portfolio renewal decision rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Tie renewals to business value: active products, future product roadmap, key markets, and whether the design supports enforcement/licensing. A periodic portfolio review (e.g., annually) prevents paying renewals for designs that no longer matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement scheduled portfolio reviews to optimize renewal spend and align protection with commercial strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most common renewal mistake for multi-country portfolios
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating all jurisdictions as if they have the same renewal rhythm and rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain jurisdiction-specific processes—some jurisdictions are annual, some in 5-year blocks, and fees/formalities differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-reduction strategies for renewals
rubrics_metrics.description: Three most common approaches are to renew only in core revenue markets, to let low-value territories lapse, and to coordinate renewals with product lifecycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize renewals by return-on-investment and product lifecycle stage to reduce portfolio maintenance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for local representative for renewals
rubrics_metrics.description: It depends on the jurisdiction and how the design was filed. Some systems allow renewal directly by the owner, while others require local representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check local rules and, if necessary, appoint local counsel/agent to handle renewals and related formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information required for quick renewals
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually the registration number, owner details (exact legal name/address), the jurisdiction, and the due date are required for renewal. For multi-country portfolios, keeping this information consistent is critical to avoid rejected renewals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep centralized records with exact legal names and dates to speed renewals and avoid administrative rejection.
